title: New fund offers residential property access
full_text:
A residential property investment firm has opened a fund that will allow SMSFs to invest in the sector without having to acquire a physical asset in a bid to meet demand following restrictions on investments via a limited recourse borrowing arrangement (LRBA).
Melbourne-based LongView stated its Home Equity Fund 2 co-invests in existing residential properties in exchange for a return of original capital and a pre-negotiated share of any future capital growth, with investors required to make a minimum investment of $100,000.
LongView executive chair James Hooke said the fund, which operates as a unit trust, provided SMSFs with the opportunity to invest in a slice of the residential property market without having to purchase an entire property and allowed trustees who could not get those types of assets into their fund portfolio to access them on a smaller and more practical scale.
“The [residential property LRBA] rule changes mean that trustees who want housing in their portfolio now need another way than directly investing in a single property,” Hooke said.
“If you decide 10 per cent of the SMSF should be in Australian residential property, there has never been a way to actually do that.
“Historically, you’ve had to commit to buying a whole house and risk that dominating your portfolio – with all of your residential property investment concentrated on a single investment – or you give up on the idea.
“Our fund allows trustees to buy into a diverse portfolio of residential housing in the size they want rather than the size that is available, without the added tax, responsibility or paperwork behind investment property ownership.”
He added the fund uses a property selection process to identify those assets with the highest chance of capital growth with a particular focus on “robust, older dwellings on well-located land”.
“Housing is driven by lots of things and despite how volatile the market seems, investing into the right kind of properties, like these, may allow your portfolio to outperform the average,” he said.
“The best solution is to own property in a more sensible portion and let someone else deal with the tenants.”
The new fund follows the release of the first Home Equity Fund in 2023, which closed oversubscribed and by 31 March 2026 had invested in more than 220 homes collectively worth $300 million and returned an average of 14.1 per cent a year since inception.
